name: aspiration-only
description: Articulate, certain, and entirely untested. Long answers produce a high evidence ceiling (moderate here, capped only by the seven-answer length), so confidence alone would happily name a direction here — which is exactly the failure blueprint 10.3 exists to prevent. The dual track must hold the line that confidence cannot: wanting it, at length, is still not having done it.
answers: I want to be a surgeon. I have wanted that since I was about eleven and I have never really considered anything else since then.
I admire doctors more than almost anyone. My uncle is one and the way people treat him when he walks into a room is something I think about a lot.
I would be good at it because I am smart and I do not get squeamish about blood or anything like that.
I have not actually done anything medical yet. My school does not have a programme and I could not get the summer placement I applied for.
I read a lot about it. I have watched every surgery documentary there is and I follow a few surgeons online.
Honestly the salary matters to me too, I am not going to pretend it does not.
I get bored in school pretty easily unless it is biology. I have not really stuck with clubs or anything outside of that.

narrative:
You have been pointed at this for five years and you can say why, which is more than most people your age can do. You also told me you have not actually done anything medical yet, and that the one placement you went after did not come through.

Those two things are not in conflict and the second is not a mark against you. It means what you have is a strong hypothesis rather than a finding. The thing that turns one into the other is contact with the actual work, and you have been blocked from that by your school rather than by anything about you.

So the next move is not more reading. It is the smallest real version of this you can get into in the next two weeks, even one that looks nothing like surgery.
